# The next number of T above a value

Kernel `next_up` · **UNVERIFIED** for finite operands · **UNVERIFIED** for infinite and NaN operands · [all operations](index.md) · [how to read this page](reading.md)

**UNVERIFIED: no proof is checked.** The statement below is a target: Rocq has not checked a proof of it. No public operation calls it yet ([What holds today](../getting-started/guarantees.md#proved-and-unverified)).

## What it computes

The next number of `T` above $a$, for every value of `T`:

$$r = \mathrm{succ}(a).$$

## C++

**Not yet called by the public headers.** No public operation computes this kernel yet.

## Requires

- Every limb of every operand is a finite number of `T`.

## Target (not proved)

When the requirements hold and no operation of the kernel overflows:

- $r = \mathrm{succ}(a)$: the next number of the format above $a$.

Stated for every binary format with a precision of at least 1 bit, rounding to nearest with ties to even and with gradual underflow, in the model where no operation overflows. Both limb types qualify: `double` has 53 bits, `float` has 24 bits.

## Status

**UNVERIFIED.** No proof of the statement is checked.

The statement, as Rocq reads it (the vocabulary, `fmt`, `RN`, `u`, `eta` and `normalized_2`, is defined at the top of the same file; `emin` is the exponent of $\eta$ and `prec` the precision):

```coq
Definition next_up_spec : Prop :=
  forall emin prec : Z, (1 <= prec)%Z ->
  forall a : R,
  fmt emin prec a ->
  let r := next_up emin prec a in
  fmt emin prec r /\
  r = succ radix2 (FLT_exp emin prec) a.
```

## Infinite and NaN operands

The statement above is about finite operands. The claims also say what the kernel returns when its operands may be infinite or NaN. That statement requires:

- $a$ is any value of `T`: a number, $\pm\infty$ or a NaN.

and then:

- $r$ is the next number of `T` above $a$: for a finite $a$ the smallest number of `T` above it, $+\infty$ above $\Omega$ and $\eta$ above either zero; $-\Omega$ for $a = -\infty$; $+\infty$ for $a = +\infty$; a NaN for a NaN.

Stated for every binary format with a precision of at least 1 bit, rounding to nearest with ties to even and with gradual underflow, in the IEEE model, with signed zeros, infinities, NaN and overflow. Both limb types qualify: `double` has 53 bits, `float` has 24 bits.

**Status of this statement: UNVERIFIED.** No proof of it is checked (`ieee_status` is `unverified` in `gen/claims.json`). The [Proofs](../proofs/index.md#what-is-proved-and-in-which-model) page says which statements of the IEEE model are proved against statements written by hand; this page gives the status that `gen/claims.json` gives.

## Source

**Algorithm:** IEEE 754 nextUp on the bit pattern (Milestone 2 listing). **License:** algorithm and proof: MIT.

## Listing

From [`gen/kernels/next_up.kernel`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/gen/kernels/next_up.kernel), the description the C++ and the formal models (`proofs/gen/Model.v`, `proofs/gen/IeeeModel.v`) are generated from. Each line is one operation of `T`; one that rounds rounds to nearest, and `prod(a, b)` is $\mathrm{RN}(ab)$, written as a fused multiply-add with a zero addend ([the kernel IR](../developer/architecture.md#the-kernel-ir)).

```
# IEEE 754 nextUp: the next number of the format above a, on every input (milestone2.md, "next_up
# and next_down on every input"). A NaN gives a NaN; +inf gives +inf; the largest finite number
# gives +inf; a positive number the next one away from zero, a negative one the next one toward
# zero; either zero the smallest positive number; -inf the most negative finite number. Computed
# on the bit pattern, without a floating-point operation.

r = succ(a)
```
